standard_text: Ray optics: reflection of light, spherical mirrors, mirror formula, refraction of light, total internal reflection and optical fibres, refraction at spherical surfaces, lenses, thin lens formula, lens maker's formula, magnification, power of a lens, combination of thin lenses in contact, refraction of light through a prism. body_html:
How to think about it

With the Cartesian sign convention, distances are measured from the pole or optical centre, and distances against the incident light are negative. Mirrors obey 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, thin lenses 1/v − 1/u = 1/f; magnification is −v/u for a mirror and v/u for a lens. Lens power P = 1/f in dioptres, and powers add for lenses in contact.

Light going from a denser to a rarer medium beyond the critical angle (sin C = 1/n) is totally internally reflected, as in optical fibres. A prism's refractive index is sin((A + D)/2)/sin(A/2). A telescope magnifies fo/fe; a simple microscope 1 + D/f.

Example

f = 20 cm, u = −30 cm, convex lens. v?

1/20 − 1/30

Answer: +60 cm

Example

f = 25 cm. P?

100 ÷ 25

Answer: +4 D

Common mistakes

  • Forgetting the sign convention.
  • Using the mirror formula for a lens.
  • Using f in cm for power.

items.q: Where must an object be placed for a convex lens to give a virtual, erect, magnified image?
c: between the lens and its focus
items.e: This is how a magnifying glass works.

items.q: A convex mirror is used as a rear-view mirror. Why?

items.e: It shows more of the road.

What is total internal reflection?
c: complete reflection of light at a boundary when it goes from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle greater than the critical angle
